I’d like to tell you a little story—one I’ve carried in my pocket like a smooth river stone, ever since I first traced its contours in a dream.

Once there was a young cartographer named Elian who lived by the edge of a vast sea. By day he mapped fishing routes and rocky shoals; by night he sketched the stars and the faint edges of unknown islands in his journals. But the most curious thing about Elian was this: he believed that somewhere, on the other side of the horizon, lay a mirror‐lake floating in mid-air. In its still waters, he was certain, the universe would reveal its hidden seams.

So one dawn, long before the gulls awoke, Elian set sail in a slender boat carved from driftwood. He followed the sun’s first light, drifting westward until the waves turned from gold to rose. Weeks went by, and the sea offered him kindly storms and phosphorescent nights, but no sky-lake. Still, he pressed on.

At last, on a morning thick with mist, Elian spotted a ring of faintly glowing mist suspended above the water—like breath frozen in the air. Heart pounding, he guided his boat underneath. The mist parted at his approach, and there it was: a pool of glass that did not rest on earth or water but floated, a perfect circle against the heavens.

Elian leaned over the rim. The face that gazed back at him was his own, framed by the endless arch of the sky, crowned by stars he’d never charted. But as he watched, the reflection shifted: constellations formed new patterns, shifting like dancers on a cosmic stage. He realized then that the mirror-lake did more than show the world; it showed his own yearning to explore, to discover, to dream anew.

He slipped his hand into those still waters—and felt them warm. The lake seemed to whisper: “Every map you draw, every line you trace, comes from this very place inside you.” Elian closed his eyes and wept, not from sorrow, but because he understood at last that the greatest journeys are the ones we make toward our own hearts.

He never did return home with charts of unknown lands. Instead, he filled his journals with poems and sketches of that floating mirror-lake—and in doing so, he invited anyone who read them to set sail on their own voyages of wonder. And perhaps that’s where you and I find ourselves now, standing at the water’s edge, learning that the horizon we chase is really the reflection of our own infinite curiosity.
